title: News Failure
teaches: The News Failure as we trade it: big, dated news meets the opposite reaction, a bad-news gap down on heavy volume that is back over the prior close by the close, above the 200-day; the buy is a market order as price trades back over the prior close, the stop sits a few cents under the news day's low (wide, so the size comes from the stop), the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working. The short is the mirror, and shorts are recommended only for traders who have already made $1 million.

steps: The short side mirrors it. SKIN, August 2022: up 54% in a run, then earnings gap it up 4.8% on 3.7x volume.
By the close it's 16.2% under the prior close, right at the low of the day, below the 200-day.
The short triggers back under the prior close, 15.26, with the stop a few cents over the day's high, 16.05.
That's 5.2%, past our 5%: we'd mostly wait. And we only recommend shorting to traders who've already made $1 million trading.

questions.q: Earnings hit before the open. What did this stock do with that news?
choices: Gapped down on bad news, closed green
Gapped up on good news, held it
Gapped down and kept falling
Drifted sideways on no news
questions.answer: Gapped down on bad news, closed green
questions.why: Gapped down on bad news and closed green. That's the whole setup. This is CELH. It opened 5.7% lower on earnings, on 7.4x its normal volume. By the close it was up 20.4% on the day. The news said sell, and the stock said no. Anyone who shorted that gap is now trapped under the price, and that's fuel. If it gaps down and stays down, the news worked. That's a different trade.
questions.lesson_line: Bad news, a gap down, and a green close. The news said sell and the stock didn't listen.

wrong.Gapped up on good news, held it: That's a News Gapper. Good news that holds is a different trade.
wrong.Gapped down and kept falling: Then the news worked. That's a bear gap, not a failure.
wrong.Drifted sideways on no news: No news, no News Failure. You need a dated headline behind a real gap.

questions.simple: It gaps down on bad news and closes back over the prior close. The bad news failed to keep it down.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed criterion (owner default, not yet ruled) (nf.scan_standin, the look-alike lines)

questions.story: Earnings came out this morning. The chart runs through the close of the news day.

questions.q: Jason Shapiro calls it a news failure when the news is bullish but the market closes down by day's end.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. That's Shapiro's own test, and he's the one who named it. In his words, by the end of the day it fails and closes down, with no other bearish news to explain it. His example adds crowded longs going into the news. Think about who's left to buy. If everyone who wanted it already owns it, good news finds no new buyers. Our long is the mirror: bad news gaps it down and it closes back over the prior close.
questions.lesson_line: The news points one way and the close goes the other. That's the tell.
questions.simple: True. Good news and a red close that day is what Shapiro calls a news failure.

reasons: same-day close test is a held decision (D-087)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A News Failure long is bought as price trades back over the ___ close.
questions.answer: prior
questions.why: Prior. The long is a market order when price trades back over the prior close on the news day, red to green. Entries are market orders. The card also allows buying at the close if you wait for Shapiro's confirmation. The trigger is not a weekly or monthly close, or a moving average.
questions.lesson_line: Buy as price trades back over the prior close.
questions.simple: Prior. You buy as the price climbs back over yesterday's close, the moment the day turns from red to green.

reasons: the red-to-green entry is a proposed card line tied to D-087

questions.q: You're in. Where does your stop go?
choices: Just under the prior day's close
A few cents under the news day's low
A few cents over the news day's high
At 3% under your buy, whatever the chart
questions.answer: A few cents under the news day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the news day's low. That low is where the sellers took their best shot. If price takes it out, the turn you bought didn't happen and you want out. The prior close is your trigger, not your stop. It's so close that normal noise shakes you out. A flat 3% ignores the chart. Then measure it. Past 5% from your buy, I mostly pass and wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Long: a few cents under the news day's low. Short: a few cents over its high.

wrong.A few cents over the news day's high: That's the short's stop. You're long, so it goes under the low.
wrong.At 3% under your buy, whatever the chart: A fixed percent ignores the chart. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong.
wrong.Just under the prior day's close: That's your trigger, not your stop. It's so close that normal noise takes you out.

questions.simple: A few cents under the news day's low. A new low means the turn you bought didn't happen.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)

questions.story: Bad news gapped this stock down at the open. You bought as it traded back over the prior close.

questions.q: If you're buying a News Failure in a single stock, it has to be trading above its 200-day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line, and a great-looking reversal doesn't change it. Under that line the big trend is down. Holders who bought higher are waiting to sell into any bounce. The only exception is an index or a levered ETF, on a reversal extension or a parabolic long. A single stock never gets that pass.
questions.lesson_line: Stocks above the 200-day only. A great reversal doesn't change that.
questions.simple: True. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, however good the reversal looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: A big gap on heavy volume only flags the day. You still need a real, dated headline behind it to call it a News Failure.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The gap and the volume tell you something hit the stock. They don't tell you what. A News Failure is about news that should have moved it and didn't. So you need the actual headline, and earnings or really notable news is what I care about. Look it up before you trade it. No headline, and it's just a red-to-green day or an Oops.
questions.lesson_line: Gap and volume flag it. The headline makes it a News Failure.
questions.simple: True. Gap and volume flag it, but a News Failure needs real news behind the gap.

reasons: the gap-and-volume stand-in is a proposed card line, not an owner ruling

questions.q: What are you looking at?
choices: A weak News Gapper
An Oops Reversal with news
A News Failure, the short side
A bear gap, the start of a fall
questions.answer: A News Failure, the short side
questions.why: A News Failure, the short side. Good news should have held it up, and it closed red, under the prior close. The buyers who paid up at the open are now holding a loss. Plenty of them will sell to get out near even. A News Gapper gets the same kind of headline but holds the gap and closes green. Shorting is only for traders who've already made $1 million. For everyone else, it's a read: good news getting sold.
questions.lesson_line: Same headline, opposite close. The gapper holds it, the failure gives it back.

wrong.A bear gap, the start of a fall: A bear gap is bad news that gaps it down and keeps it down. This was good news.
wrong.A weak News Gapper: A News Gapper holds the gap and closes green. This one gave it all back and more.
wrong.An Oops Reversal with news: An Oops opens under the prior day's low. This one gapped up.

questions.simple: Good news gapped it up and it still closed under the prior close. That's a News Failure, the short side.

reasons: the same-day close test is a held decision (D-087)

questions.story: Good news gapped this stock up at the open. By the close it was back under the prior day's close.

questions.q: Earnings gap a stock down. It closes at the low of the day and keeps sliding the next morning. What is it?
choices: A News Failure long on the open
A News Gapper that held its gap
A Red to Green on the second day
A bear gap or earnings breakdown
questions.answer: A bear gap or earnings breakdown
questions.why: A bear gap, an earnings breakdown. The bad news worked. Sellers hit it at the open and kept hitting it into the close. There's no failure here to buy. The News Failure long needs the opposite: price back over the prior close the same day. Call this a News Failure and buy it, and you're catching a falling knife. I'd leave it alone.
questions.lesson_line: If the gap down keeps going, the news worked. Leave it.

wrong.A News Failure long on the open: The long needs a close back over the prior close. This one closed at the low.
wrong.A News Gapper that held its gap: A News Gapper is good news that holds. This was bad news.
wrong.A Red to Green on the second day: Red to Green means trading back over the prior close. It never got there.

questions.simple: A bear gap. The bad news worked and the stock stayed down, so there's no failure to buy.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's look-alike lines and listed mistake (house source)

questions.q: Say you trade shorts. How do you get in on this one?
choices: Market, over the prior day's high
Market, back under the prior close
A limit order at the day's high
Market, at the open into the gap up
questions.answer: Market, back under the prior close
questions.why: Market order as it trades back under the prior close. That's green to red, the moment the good news actually fails. Shorting the open bets against the news before it's failed. The market hasn't shown you anything yet. A limit at the high waits for a price that may never come back. Your stop goes a few cents over the news day's high. And shorting is only for traders who've already made $1 million.
questions.lesson_line: Short it green to red, through the prior close. Never into the open gap.

wrong.Market, over the prior day's high: That's a breakout trigger for a long. The short's trigger is the prior close.
wrong.A limit order at the day's high: We use market orders when the trigger trades. A limit at the high may never fill.
wrong.Market, at the open into the gap up: That shorts the good news before it's failed. Wait for the trade back under the prior close.

questions.simple: Market order as it trades back under the prior close. That's the moment the good news fails.

deeper.trap: Shorting the open into good news bets against it before it has failed. The market has shown you nothing yet. Wait for the failure itself: price trading back under the prior close, green to red. Until then there's no trade.

reasons: the short entry is a proposed card line; traded shorts wait on D-001

questions.story: Good news gapped this stock up at the open. Then it sold off all day.

questions.q: On one day, dozens of stocks gap up on good news and close red. That's a market story, not dozens of separate shorts.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. One stock fading good news tells you about that stock. Dozens doing it on the same day tells you the news was the market. On April 8, 2025 there were 56 of them, in a washed-out market. The market rallied hard the next day. So read a cluster like that as one market read. Shorting the whole list is one bet placed many times.
questions.lesson_line: One stock fading good news is a stock story. Dozens is a market story.
questions.simple: True. When many stocks fade good news on one day, the cause is the market, not each stock.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed criterion (owner default, not yet ruled) (nf.not_market_wide)

questions.q: This $7 stock trades $8 million a day and just made a clean News Failure. What's our minimum to even look at it?
choices: $5 and $5 million a day
$20 and $100 million a day
$10 and $20 million a day
$10 and 1 million shares a day
questions.answer: $10 and $20 million a day
questions.why: $10 a share and $20 million traded a day. This one fails both, so it's a pass. Thin stocks gap through your stop, and you can't get out at your price. A few big orders push them around. The $20 million is dollars traded, not shares. A million shares of a $7 stock is only $7 million. I'd rather trade a liquid name than a pretty chart I can't get out of.
questions.lesson_line: $10 and $20 million a day, or it's not on the list.

wrong.$5 and $5 million a day: Way too thin. Our floor is $10 and $20 million a day.
wrong.$20 and $100 million a day: That's stricter than our floor of $10 and $20 million a day.
wrong.$10 and 1 million shares a day: Close, but the floor is dollars traded, $20 million, not a share count.

questions.simple: At least $10 a share and $20 million traded a day. Thin stocks are hard to get out of.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: No new buy or short in the ___ sessions before a scheduled report.
questions.why: 3. No new buy or short in the 3 sessions before a scheduled report. Our rulebook says the same for buys: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A trade already on is held through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Three sessions before a report, no new trade.
questions.simple: 3. We open no new trade in the 3 sessions before a scheduled report.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: Bad news gaps your stock down and it comes all the way back. Where do you want it to close?
choices: Near the low of the day
Right on the prior close
Near the high of the day
Anywhere green, by a few cents
questions.answer: Near the high of the day
questions.why: Near the high of the day. That's the full reversal: the whole gap erased, and buyers still paying up into the bell. Sellers had all day to push it back down and couldn't. If it also closes over yesterday's high, even better. AAOI did it after a flush under the prior day's low, closing 20.3% over the prior close near the high. Green by a few cents still counts. It's a draw though, not a win. Grading's a judgment call, so read the bar by eye.
questions.lesson_line: Gap erased, close near the high. That's the one I want.

wrong.Near the low of the day: That's the short's shape. Sellers still won the day.
wrong.Right on the prior close: The long needs a close back over the prior close. Flat on it isn't a failure yet.
wrong.Anywhere green, by a few cents: It counts, but barely. A close near the high is the stronger read.

questions.simple: Near the high of the day. The gap is erased and buyers held it into the close.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's proposed criterion (owner default, not yet ruled) (nf.grade_shape)

questions.q: Jason Shapiro will take a trade on crowded positioning alone, without waiting for the news to fail.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Shapiro needs both. In his words, trader positioning is not enough to execute the trade. You also need market confirmation. The crowd all leaning one way tells you the fuel is there. The news failure tells you it's starting to burn. A crowd can stay crowded for months. So he waits for the market to show him.
questions.lesson_line: Crowding is the fuel. The failed news is the match.
questions.simple: False. Shapiro says crowding alone isn't enough, so he waits for the market to confirm it.

questions.q: When is it too far gone to buy?
choices: More than 4% past the prior close
More than 10% past the prior close
Never, the stop handles it
More than 4% past the day's low
questions.answer: More than 4% past the prior close
questions.why: Once it's more than 4% over the prior close, I let it go. On the long the prior close is the trigger, so that's where you measure from, not the day's low. Your stop still sits a few cents under the news day's low. Every cent you chase pushes that stop further away. Same risk, so the size has to shrink. You pay more for the same trade and own less of it. Missing one costs you nothing.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, let it go. Another one comes.

wrong.More than 10% past the prior close: Way too loose. Past 4% you're already chasing.
wrong.Never, the stop handles it: The stop doesn't fix a chase. It just sits farther away, so you buy fewer shares.
wrong.More than 4% past the day's low: You measure from the trigger, the prior close, not from the low.

questions.simple: More than 4% over the prior close, you skip it. Chasing pushes your stop away and shrinks your size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.story: A News Failure long triggered this morning as it traded back over the prior close. You were away from the screen. It's well above that close now.

questions.q: How far is that stop from the buy?
questions.why: 5.7%. 86.36 minus 81.48 is 4.88 a share. 4.88 over 86.36, times 100, is 5.7%. That's past the 5% I'll accept. I like 1 to 3%. Past 5%, I mostly wait for a tighter trigger instead of taking it. Don't fix it by pulling the stop up. That just parks it inside the day's noise. AAOI ran to 30.2R, but you don't get to know that at the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop in percent before you buy. Past 5%, mostly wait.
questions.simple: 5.7%. That's past the 5% we accept, so you'd mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

deeper.trap: A wide stop tempts you to pull it closer so your normal size fits. Don't. The stop stays a few cents under the news day's low, and the size comes from it. If that doesn't fit, you skip it or wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A13)

wrong.6.0%: You divided by the stop, 81.48, instead of the buy.
wrong.4.9%: That's the dollar gap, 4.88, read as a percent.
wrong.0.6%: The decimal slipped a place. It's 5.7%.

questions.story: Bad news gapped this leader down, and it traded back over the prior close at 86.36. The news day's low puts the stop at 81.48.

questions.q: You bought a News Failure at 40.00 with the stop at 38.00. Where's 3R?
questions.why: 46.00. 40.00 minus 38.00 is 2.00 a share. That's 1R. Three of those is 6.00. Add it to your 40.00 buy and you get 46.00. Know where 3R and 5R are before you buy, so you can see how the trade's doing. 3R isn't an automatic sell, though. I'd rather sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push than at a fixed mark.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before you buy. It's a mark to measure by, not a sell order.
questions.simple: $46.00. One R is 2.00, three of them is 6.00, added to your 40.00 buy.

deeper.example: SEDG on 2025-11-05 was bought at 31.83 with the stop at 30.23, a 5.0% stop. It reached 3R the next day, and its best move reached 10.5R.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

wrong.$48.00: That's four R. One too many.
wrong.$52.00: You doubled the R before adding three of them.
wrong.$120.00: You multiplied the buy by three. R is the stop distance.

questions.q: Shapiro only gets out if a day closes past the failure day's extreme. How does your stop work on a News Failure?
choices: Same, only on a close past it
A mental stop I watch all day
A real stop order, hit intraday
No stop, a small size caps it
questions.answer: A real stop order, hit intraday
questions.why: A real stop order with your broker, and it can fill during the day. Every position gets one. A stop in your head is a stop you'll argue with when price gets there. Shapiro's close-only stop is his way. It tested no better, so it isn't ours. It also lets a bad day run well past your level before you're out.
questions.lesson_line: Real stop order, in with the broker. Not in your head.

wrong.Same, only on a close past it: That's Shapiro's way. It tested no better, and a bad day can run far past your level.
wrong.A mental stop I watch all day: A stop in your head gets argued with. Put the order in.
wrong.No stop, a small size caps it: Small size doesn't stop a collapse. Every position gets a real stop order.

questions.simple: A real stop order sits with your broker and fills during the day. Not a mental stop, not close-only.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D41)

questions.q: Your News Failure long keeps dipping toward your stop. Moving the stop a bit lower to give it room is fine.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. You set it under the news day's low because that's where you're wrong. Price getting close doesn't change that. Lowering it just turns a planned loss into a bigger one. The only time a stop moves lower is a gap through it. Then the first 30-minute low is the new stop, and you're out if that's past 2R.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves your way. Never wider.
questions.simple: False. The stop only moves up, and lowering it turns a planned loss into a bigger one.

deeper.trap: Widening a stop that keeps getting close turns a planned loss into a bigger one. The only time a stop moves wider is a gap through it, and even then a loss past 2R means out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.q: You sold some of your News Failure into a push. How do you manage what's left?
choices: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
A close under the 200-day
A fixed 5% under the high
An intraday touch of the 9 EMA
questions.answer: A close under the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: Trail it with a close under the 9 or 20 EMA. A fast mover gets the 9, a steadier one the 20. It takes a close under the line, not a touch. Stocks wick through the 9 all the time and finish above it. The line rises with the stock, so your exit keeps climbing. The 200-day is far too loose for that. A fixed 5% ignores how the stock trades.
questions.lesson_line: What's left rides the 9 or 20 EMA until it closes under it.

wrong.An intraday touch of the 9 EMA: Stocks wick through the 9 all the time. It takes a close under it.
wrong.A close under the 200-day: Way too loose. You'd hand back most of the move.
wrong.A fixed 5% under the high: A fixed percent ignores how the stock moves. The rising average does that for you.

questions.simple: Sell the rest on a daily close under the 9 EMA for a fast mover, or the 20 EMA for a steadier one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: You're long a News Failure and it gaps down through your stop at the open. Where's your stop now?
choices: The prior close or the open
The low of the first 30 minutes
The 9 EMA at the open
The low of the first 5 minutes
questions.answer: The low of the first 30 minutes
questions.why: The low of the first 30 minutes. The gap already jumped your level, so the price you planned on is gone. Instead of dumping it at the open, let the first 30 minutes show you where it holds. That low becomes the new stop. There's a ceiling, though. If that low puts the loss past 2R, you're out. It's the one time a stop moves lower, and the gap moved it, not you.
questions.lesson_line: Gap through the stop, and the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.The 9 EMA at the open: The 9 EMA is your trail, not the gap stop.
wrong.The prior close or the open: Neither. The first 30 minutes set the new stop.
wrong.The low of the first 5 minutes: Five minutes is mostly noise. Use the first 30.

questions.simple: The low of the first 30 minutes becomes your stop. If that loss is past 2R, you get out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

questions.q: Ten sessions in, your News Failure is up only half an R. You keep holding until the stop or the trail takes you out.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Under 1R after 10 trading days, it's sold. The idea was a sharp turn, and it hasn't come. Meanwhile that money is stuck in a trade going nowhere. It could be in one that's working. So sell it, free the money, and move on.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions under 1R, and the money moves on.
questions.simple: False. Still under 1R after 10 sessions, you sell it and free the money for something that's working.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Does the day pass the gap-and-volume test for news?
choices: No; the gap down is under 4%
No; volume must be 10x the average
Yes; the gap and volume both clear
Yes; the 6.6x volume alone is enough
questions.answer: Yes; the gap and volume both clear
questions.why: Yes. The open is 6.2% under the prior close, more than the 4% the test asks. Volume is 6.6 times the 50-day average, over the 2 times the test asks. Both parts must clear. Passing only flags the day; the reversal back over the prior close is still needed.
questions.lesson_line: A gap of 4% or more on 2 times the volume passes the test.

wrong.No; the gap down is under 4%: The open is more than 4% under the prior close, so it clears 4%.
wrong.No; volume must be 10x the average: The test asks for 2 times the 50-day volume or more.
wrong.Yes; the 6.6x volume alone is enough: Volume alone does not pass. The test also needs an open 4% or more under the prior close.

questions.story: An earnings day. It opens 6.2% under the prior close on 6.6x its 50-day average volume.
questions.simple: Yes. The open is over 4% under the prior close, and volume is more than twice the 50-day average.

reasons: the gap-and-volume stand-in is a proposed card line
the key rests on arithmetic from the story

questions.q: Is this a News Failure, or just a Red to Green?
choices: Just a Red to Green, no news
A News Failure, it reclaimed
Neither, it never closed green
A News Failure, any gap counts
questions.answer: Just a Red to Green, no news
questions.why: Just a Red to Green. The trigger's the same, price trading back over the prior close, and you can buy it as one. But there's no news here to fail. A 1% dip on normal volume with no headline is just a soft open. A News Failure needs a headline that should have hurt it, and a real gap down on it. That's sellers really trying and losing. Heavy volume behind the gap raises the grade on top.
questions.lesson_line: Same trigger. The headline and the gap make it a News Failure.

wrong.A News Failure, it reclaimed: Reclaiming the close is the trigger, not the setup. There's no news behind this dip.
wrong.Neither, it never closed green: It traded back over the prior close. That's a Red to Green.
wrong.A News Failure, any gap counts: A soft 1% open with no headline isn't news. Nothing failed.

questions.story: A stock dips 1% at the open on normal volume. There's no headline anywhere. By lunch it's back over the prior close.
questions.simple: Just a Red to Green. Same trigger, but no headline and no real gap, so there's no news to fail.

deeper.trap: The bar alone can fool you, because the trigger is the same. What changes is the story behind the gap: real news and a real gap down. Without those it's a plain Red to Green.

reasons: the 4% news gap is a proposed card line

questions.q: News Gapper or News Failure?
choices: News Gapper; the headline was good
News Failure; it closed red
Bear gap; the stock fell
questions.answer: News Failure; it closed red
questions.why: News Failure. Good news gapped it up and it closed red, under the prior close. A News Gapper holds the gap.
questions.lesson_line: Read the close against the prior close. Same headline, opposite trade.

wrong.News Gapper; the headline was good: A News Gapper closes green and holds the gap. This one closed red.
wrong.Bear gap; the stock fell: A bear gap starts with bad news. This was good news.

questions.story: A contract headline gaps a stock up 8%, and it closes 2% under the prior close.

questions.q: News Failure or earnings breakdown?
choices: News Failure; the headline was bad
News Gapper; the gap was big
Earnings breakdown; the news worked
questions.answer: Earnings breakdown; the news worked
questions.why: Earnings breakdown. Bad news gapped it down and it stayed down, so the news worked.
questions.lesson_line: If the gap keeps going, the news worked. Don't call it a failure.

wrong.News Failure; the headline was bad: A News Failure long closes back over the prior close. This one stayed down.
wrong.News Gapper; the gap was big: A News Gapper is a good-news gap that holds.

questions.story: An earnings miss gaps a stock down 9%. It closes at the low of the day, near the open.

questions.q: Which setup are you trading here?
choices: An Oops, there's no catalyst
A News Failure, it reclaimed
A News Failure, it opened low
Neither, an Oops needs news
questions.answer: An Oops, there's no catalyst
questions.why: An Oops. It opened under the prior day's low and took back the prior close, and an Oops doesn't need news. A News Failure does. It's about a headline that should have moved the stock and didn't. With nothing behind the gap, there's no news to fail. You'd still buy it as an Oops, through the prior close. An Oops on a real news day is both at once.
questions.lesson_line: No headline, no News Failure. That's an Oops.

wrong.A News Failure, it reclaimed: Reclaiming is the trigger. With no headline, there's no news to fail.
wrong.A News Failure, it opened low: Opening under the prior low is the Oops part. It still needs news to be a News Failure.
wrong.Neither, an Oops needs news: An Oops needs no news. Just the open under the low and the trade back over the close.

questions.story: No headline, no earnings, nothing. A stock opens under yesterday's low, then trades back over yesterday's close.
questions.simple: An Oops. It needs no news, and a News Failure needs a real headline behind the gap.

reasons: what counts as news is a held decision (D-032)

questions.q: What does that tell you about the news?
choices: Twelve strong signals; short them all
The news was the market, not one stock
